CORRECTION — the widely reported 'AEP Ohio: 85% minimum demand over 12 years above 25 MW' is wrong in two of its three numbers. 85% is not the floor: for New Load between 25,001 kW and 75,000 kW the Minimum Demand is 15,000 kW plus 85% of the marginal amount over 25,000 kW, so a 25 MW customer's floor is 15 MW, i.e. 60% of contract capacity; above 75,000 kW the marginal rate is 100%, not 85%, subject to an overall 85%-of-contract-capacity cap. And the term is the Load Ramp Period plus 8 years, which equals 12 only when the ramp runs its full 4 years. Existing Load sits at a 60% floor throughout. Verified against Schedule DCT Original Sheets 223-1 through 223-7.

The award record shows $894,733,810 already obligated and a base-and-all-options value of $3,082,072,958, making this by a wide margin the largest single utility vehicle surfaced in this sweep. A companion contract to the same recipient on the same day (SP0600-07-C-8261) carries a further $212,665,748 obligated. The contractor is a regulated utility: its rates at these installations are set by the Regulatory Commission of Alaska, not by the contract alone.
records.microreactor_read: This is the instrument a microreactor should be sold into rather than around: a single counterparty already holds a fifty-year, three-billion-dollar franchise to supply heat and power to Alaska Army installations, and its generation is coal and oil in a place where fuel arrives by rail and barge. The reactor does not need to beat a $/kW number to enter — it needs to become an asset inside a rate base a regulator already approves, and the addressable line is the roughly $60M a year of obligations this one contract has averaged since 2007.

records.summary: NAVFAC EXWC issued Ameresco a task order under the DOE ESPC IDIQ on 2016-12-28 to build and then operate a site-wide microgrid at Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island, with a period of performance running to 2041-11-30. Ameresco announced the deal as a $91.1 million self-funding ESPC covering 10 MW of new on-site generation, a 3.5 MW gas CHP plant replacing the end-of-life steam plant, 6.7 MW-DC of solar PV and an 8.0 MWh battery. The federal award record tells a different story about size: $66,631,952 has been obligated so far and the contract's base-and-all-options value is $212,716,674 — 2.3x the announced $91.1M, because the ESPC's later years are performance-period service payments, not construction. The host pays nothing up front and repays out of guaranteed savings across roughly 25 years.
records.microreactor_read: Two numbers matter to a microreactor seller here and they are far apart: the capital comparison is $91.1M for about 10 MW of mixed generation, i.e. roughly $9,100/kW nameplate and about $26,000/kW if you count only the 3.5 MW of firm dispatchable CHP; the commercial comparison is the $212.7M of lifecycle contract value a 25-year vehicle at one recruit depot can actually carry. A 5-10 MW microreactor priced against the $91.1M sticker looks expensive and priced against the $212.7M lifecycle envelope looks financeable — which is why the instrument, not the capex, is the thing to copy.

records.summary: In July 2019 NAVFAC Southeast awarded Siemens Government Technologies an ESPC task order — announced at $828.8 million and issued for 25 years of construction plus operation — to replace diesel generation at Naval Station Guantanamo Bay with a dual-fuel LNG combined-cycle plant and a solar field. The federal award record shows $101,059,504 obligated so far against a base-and-all-options value of $927,391,394 with a potential end date of 2043-04-24, so the contract has grown roughly $100M past its announced value and only about 11 percent of the ceiling has been obligated. records.microreactor_read: Guantanamo is the strongest capex-per-MW argument in this file and it runs the reactor's way: $368.8M for 20 MW of island generation is $18,440/kW, and that is for a gas plant whose fuel still has to arrive by ship. A 1-20 MW microreactor competing at an isolated base does not need to beat $5,400/kW — at a site with no pipeline and no grid tie it needs to beat roughly $18,000/kW plus a fuel logistics chain, against a counterfactual the Navy itself valued at $24.6M a year in savings over 22 years.

records.summary: The Regulatory Commission of Alaska set the FY2024 Power Cost Equalization base rate at $0.1935/kWh on 13 June 2023 and, a week later, recalculated the per-kWh PCE credit for every participating rural utility. The attached Appendix 1 sheets are the single best published price-to-beat dataset in US remote power: for each utility they state test-period kWh sales, non-fuel power cost per kWh, fuel/purchased-power cost per kWh, and total power cost per kWh. Total power costs run from about $0.41/kWh at wind-equipped Kotzebue to $1.9487/kWh at Lime Village, with fuel alone above $0.81/kWh at Igiugig and $1.52/kWh at Lime Village. The state pays the gap above the base rate up to a statutory ceiling of $1.00/kWh of total cost, so any community whose costs exceed roughly $1.00/kWh is already eating unsubsidised cost.
records.microreactor_read: This is the price sheet. A 1-20 MW reactor selling into rural Alaska must beat a delivered cost of service that the regulator itself certifies at $0.62-$1.95/kWh, with the fuel-only component alone at $0.38-$1.53/kWh in the villages - but the loads are tiny (Igiugig 272 MWh/yr, Kokhanok 359 MWh/yr), so only aggregated or hub communities like Kotzebue (19.7 GWh/yr, and already down at $0.41/kWh because of wind) present a load a reactor could actually serve. The commercially interesting band is the mid-size hub at $0.60-$1.00/kWh, not the cheapest and not the smallest.

records.summary: On 11 June 2025 the Defense Logistics Agency Energy, acting for the Department of the Air Force, issued a Notice of Intent to Award to Oklo for the DoD's first commercial microreactor. The structure is a build-own-operate arrangement: Oklo would design, construct, own and operate the plant and sell electricity and steam to the base under a long-term, firm-fixed-price power purchase agreement reported at 30 years. Capacity is up to 5 MWe, sitting alongside Eielson's existing 23 MW coal-fired plant. No price has been published; the rate for power is explicitly left to contract negotiation, and the award is contingent on Oklo obtaining an NRC licence.
records.microreactor_read: This is the cleanest template for selling a 1-20 MW reactor into a remote outpost: the host buys energy, not a reactor, on a 30-year firm-fixed-price PPA from a private owner-operator, contracted by a central buying agency (DLA Energy) rather than the base. The commercially important gap is that no price is published, so the deal proves the instrument exists but sets no benchmark - and the reactor is sized at 5 MW against a 23 MW incumbent, i.e. it is a supplement, not a replacement.

records.summary: The single most useful disclosure in this sector. TUGLIQ's federally funded completion report for the Raglan wind-storage pilot states the northern power price band outright: rates range from $1.20/kWh at the high end to $0.20/kWh at the low end, and industrial self-generators - i.e. mines running their own diesel plants - average $0.25 to $0.60/kWh even with grouped purchasing. Against that, a C$20 million, 3 MW turbine with flywheel, lithium and hydrogen storage was projected to return C$41 million in fuel and O&M savings over 20 years at a mine burning ~60 million litres of diesel a year. Ottawa funded C$7.8 million of the pilot and returned with C$3.9 million and a further C$7.1 million for the Raglan 2.0 expansion.
records.microreactor_read: This is the number to beat, from a Government of Canada report rather than a vendor deck: $0.25-$0.60/kWh for an industrial self-generator in the Canadian North, with the tail up to $1.20/kWh. A 5 MW microreactor selling at even $0.30/kWh into a Raglan-class site clears the low end of that band, and the Raglan precedent shows the miner will let a third party own the asset and take federal money to de-risk the first unit. The binding constraint is not price - it is that Raglan's own report frames micro-grid collapse (ventilation loss at -40C) as the reason northern operators distrust new generation, so a reactor must prove it firms the grid rather than adding a new failure mode.

KGHM - a copper miner that also runs smelters and refineries - signed with NuScale in February 2022, executed a Task Order and Statement of Commencement under an Early Works Agreement in September 2022 at the Karpacz Economic Forum, applied to Poland's National Atomic Energy Agency for a 462 MWe six-module plant, and received the decision-in-principle in July 2023, the first step in Poland's permit chain for nuclear facilities. records.microreactor_read: The instructive part is the size: the miner that actually went nuclear specified 462 MWe, not 5 or 20, because its load is smelting and refining rather than a mill on a diesel microgrid. Mineral processing - not mining - is where the megawatts are, and it is usually grid-connected, so the reactor competes against a wholesale tariff rather than the $0.25-$0.60/kWh diesel band. For a 1-20 MW unit the read is negative on this precedent and positive on the pattern: process heat and refinery load justify nuclear at a miner's board, while a pit and a mill alone have not yet done so anywhere.

records.summary: The direct competitor to a microreactor at Canada's most diesel-exposed mines is a wire, and it is priced. Nunavut's minister responsible for Qulliq Energy told the legislature in June 2025 that the Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link now costs an estimated C$3.2 billion, up from C$1.2 billion in 2019, for a 1,200 km line from Gillam, Manitoba to five Kivalliq communities, completion pushed to 2032. Priced against NRCan's C$200-350m for a 20 MWe mining SMR, a handful of on-site units would cover the mine's load for a small fraction of the line's cost and years sooner. What the reactor cannot buy is the rest of the package: the line also takes five Inuit communities off diesel under Inuit ownership, which is what is actually mobilising the public money.
